names.name: the one self (eka ātman) of the deity, praised in many ways
the great god (mahān devaḥ) who is speech, entering mortals
the imperishable (akṣara), reached by the higher knowledge

descriptions: Because of the deity's great majesty the one self is praised in many ways; the other gods are its limbs (Nirukta 7.4).
The deities are three by station yet may be taken as person-like, not person-like, or both (Nirukta 7.5–7).
Grammar is studied so that we may become equal to the great god, speech (Mahābhāṣya, Paspaśā).
The Vedas and their six limbs are the lower knowledge; the higher is that by which the imperishable is attained (MuU 1.1.4–5).
relation_to_self: The seers saw the hymns when Brahman came upon them (Nirukta 2.11); some hymns speak in the first person of the self (ādhyātmika, Nirukta 7.1).
relation_to_world: The gods and their powers are the limbs and functions of one self; time, the year and its cycle are presided over by Prajāpati (VJ Ṛk 1).
caveat: The Vedāṅgas describe themselves as lower knowledge and posit no systematic doctrine of the ultimate; the grammarians' śabda-brahman belongs to lin:vyakarana (U31). They would not accept a one-truth reading that loosens the exact letter, accent and sequence of the Veda, which must be preserved as it is.

descriptions: The ruler of all, subtler than the subtle, bright as gold, graspable by a mind as if in sleep (MDh 12.122).
Some call him Agni, others Manu, Prajāpati, Indra, the breath, the eternal Brahman (MDh 12.123).
He pervades all beings with the five elements and turns them like a wheel through birth, growth and decay (MDh 12.124).
The self is one and yet many, like space in pots or the sun reflected in many waters (YS 3.144).
All living beings are the city of the one who lies in the cave, unslain and stainless (ĀpDh 1.8.22).
relation_to_self: Seeing the self by yoga is the highest dharma (YS 1.8); knowledge of the self is the highest of all means (MDh 12.85); the self is its own witness (MDh 8.84); seeing the self in all beings one reaches Brahman (MDh 12.125).
relation_to_world: The world issues from the self-existent (MDh 1.5–6) and revolves through ages and Manu-periods (MDh 1.68–80); dharma differs by age.
caveat: Dharmaśāstra itself states the many-names principle (MDh 12.123) but insists that knowledge of the one does not dissolve the duties of class and life-stage before liberation — the debts must be paid first (MDh 6.35–37) — and the 'one-order' teachers subordinate renunciation and liberation to the householder's dharma.
